collection: NCEE Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude: journeys and produce preservation
note: Original four-option practice for final-year primary pupils. Historical topic references are provisional. Preservation items are conceptual. Independent academic review pending.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.learningObjective: Relate total distance and elapsed time to average speed and compare journey plans.
questions.prompt: A minibus travelled 24 km before a stop and 36 km after it. From departure to arrival, including the stop, it took 90 minutes. What was its average speed for the whole trip?
options: 40 km/h
30 km/h
60 km/h
90 km/h
questions.explanation: The distance was 60 km and 90 minutes is 1½ hours. Dividing 60 by 1½ gives 40 km/h.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.learningObjective: Relate total distance and elapsed time to average speed and compare journey plans.
questions.prompt: Two riders travelled from the same starting point to the same finish along the same route. Hauwa left at 07:15 and arrived at 08:05. Timi left at 07:30 and arrived at 08:10. Which statement is correct?
questions.answer: Timi had the greater average speed because he covered the same distance in less time.
options: Hauwa had the greater average speed because she arrived first.
Timi had the greater average speed because he covered the same distance in less time.
Their average speeds were equal because they covered the same distance.
Hauwa had the greater average speed because she left earlier.
questions.explanation: Hauwa took 50 minutes and Timi took 40 minutes. For equal distances, the shorter elapsed time gives the greater average speed.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.learningObjective: Relate total distance and elapsed time to average speed and compare journey plans.
questions.prompt: A food delivery van must complete an 84 km route in 2 hours. It covers the first 36 km in 1 hour. What average speed must it maintain over the remaining distance to finish on time?
options: 36 km/h
42 km/h
48 km/h
84 km/h
questions.explanation: The remaining distance is 84 − 36 = 48 km. There is one hour left, so the required average is 48 km/h.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.learningObjective: Relate total distance and elapsed time to average speed and compare journey plans.
questions.prompt: A pupil records a complete bicycle trip as 9 km at an average of 18 km/h. Which line belongs in the trip log for elapsed time?
options: 9 minutes
18 minutes
120 minutes
30 minutes
questions.explanation: Elapsed time equals distance divided by average speed. The result is ½ hour, or 30 minutes.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.learningObjective: Relate total distance and elapsed time to average speed and compare journey plans.
questions.prompt: A bus takes 2 hours to cover 120 km. An extra stop would make the same journey last 2½ hours. By how much would the average speed fall?
options: 12 km/h
6 km/h
24 km/h
48 km/h
questions.explanation: The original average is 60 km/h. The new average is 48 km/h, a fall of 12 km/h.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.learningObjective: Relate total distance and elapsed time to average speed and compare journey plans.
questions.prompt: A courier cycles at a steady 12 km/h for 45 minutes, then walks beside the bicycle at 4 km/h for 15 minutes. How far does the courier travel altogether?
options: 8 km
10 km
12 km
16 km
questions.explanation: The cycling distance is 12 × ¾ = 9 km. The walking distance is 4 × ¼ = 1 km. Together they make 10 km.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.subtopic: Purpose and principles of produce preservation
questions.learningObjective: Recognise purposes and familiar preservation methods and interpret observations about storage losses.
questions.prompt: A pepper grower expects to sell only part of a large harvest on market day. Why plan to preserve some of the harvest?
questions.answer: It can reduce losses and make some produce available after market day.
options: It increases the number of peppers already harvested.
It makes the remaining peppers grow faster after picking.
It can reduce losses and make some produce available after market day.
It removes all costs of transporting the harvest.
questions.explanation: Preservation can slow spoilage, leaving more of the existing harvest available for later use.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.subtopic: Purpose and principles of produce preservation
questions.learningObjective: Recognise purposes and familiar preservation methods and interpret observations about storage losses.
questions.prompt: A class compares an illustration of fresh sliced okra with one of dried okra. Which change is most directly related to drying as a preservation method?
questions.answer: Less water remains in the okra.
options: The slices gain water from the air.
The seeds inside the okra become larger.
The colour alone keeps the okra from changing.
Less water remains in the okra.
questions.explanation: Drying removes moisture. The reduction in moisture, rather than a colour change, explains its role in preservation.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.subtopic: Purpose and principles of produce preservation
questions.learningObjective: Recognise purposes and familiar preservation methods and interpret observations about storage losses.
questions.prompt: Two equal batches of dry maize were put into similar stores. The store with a damaged door had more grains showing signs of pest damage. Which observation would best help check whether the damaged door mattered?
questions.answer: Look for openings around the door and signs of pests near them.
options: Look for openings around the door and signs of pests near them.
Compare the paint colours on the roofs.
Measure how far each store is from the market.
Count how many sacks were delivered last year.
questions.explanation: Openings and pest signs would help establish whether pests might have entered through the damaged door. The difference in damage alone does not prove the route.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.subtopic: Purpose and principles of produce preservation
questions.learningObjective: Recognise purposes and familiar preservation methods and interpret observations about storage losses.
questions.prompt: A farm is comparing two ways to store produce. One batch was already bruised and the other was undamaged before storage. What makes this a poor comparison?
questions.answer: Initial damage could affect the results as well as the storage methods.
options: The two methods must always give identical results.
Initial damage could affect the results as well as the storage methods.
Bruising can only occur after produce enters storage.
Counting spoiled pieces would conceal the storage methods entirely.
questions.explanation: A difference observed later cannot be attributed confidently to storage if the batches started in different conditions.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.subtopic: Purpose and principles of produce preservation
questions.learningObjective: Recognise purposes and familiar preservation methods and interpret observations about storage losses.
questions.prompt: A display describes a cool store used to hold vegetables before delivery. What does refrigeration chiefly do in that example?
questions.answer: It keeps produce at a lower temperature, slowing many changes that cause spoilage.
options: It dries the vegetables completely while they are in the store.
It restores freshness to vegetables that have already spoiled.
It keeps produce at a lower temperature, slowing many changes that cause spoilage.
It makes vegetables keep indefinitely at any temperature.
questions.explanation: Cooling can slow deterioration. It does not reverse spoilage or make storage time unlimited.

questions.subject: Quantitative and Vocational Aptitude
questions.subtopic: Purpose and principles of produce preservation
questions.learningObjective: Recognise purposes and familiar preservation methods and interpret observations about storage losses.
questions.prompt: A cooperative wants to compare how much produce was lost under two storage plans. The plans started with different quantities. What should it compare?
questions.answer: The share of the starting quantity lost under each plan.
options: Only the weight of the largest crate.
Only the number of crates left, regardless of starting stock.
The amount of floor space under each stack of crates.
The share of the starting quantity lost under each plan.
questions.explanation: Expressing the loss as a share of each starting quantity puts the two plans on a comparable basis.
